title: Algorithms & Data Structures for System Design
summary: Probabilistic data structures (Bloom filter, Count-Min Sketch, HyperLogLog), spatial data structures (Quadtree, GeoHash, R-tree), and algorithmic building blocks used in large-scale systems.

explanation.overview: Certain algorithmic building blocks appear repeatedly in system design. Bloom filters tell you if an element is NOT in a set (with zero false negatives). HyperLogLog counts unique elements in constant memory. Quadtrees and GeoHashes enable proximity search. Understanding these gives you powerful tools for interviews.

key_concepts.definition: Space-efficient probabilistic set membership test. Answers 'is X in the set?' with two possible results: DEFINITELY NOT (100% accurate) or PROBABLY YES (false positive possible). INTERNAL: a bit array of m bits (all 0 initially) + k independent hash functions. INSERT(x): compute k hashes → set bits at those k positions to 1. LOOKUP(x): compute k hashes → check if ALL k positions are 1. If any is 0, x is DEFINITELY NOT in the set. If all are 1, x is PROBABLY in the set (could be a collision). FALSE POSITIVE RATE: p ≈ (1 - e^(-kn/m))^k. For 1% false positive rate with 1M elements: m ≈ 9.6M bits (1.2 MB), k ≈ 7 hash functions. CANNOT DELETE elements (setting a bit to 0 affects other elements that hash to the same bit). FIX: Counting Bloom Filter (each position is a counter instead of a bit — increment on insert, decrement on delete). USE CASES: (1) Chrome Safe Browsing: checks URLs against a Bloom filter of known malicious URLs before querying the server. (2) Cassandra/HBase: checks if an SSTable might contain a key before reading from disk. (3) Spell checkers: check if a word is NOT in the dictionary. (4) Weak password check: check if password is in the list of compromised passwords.

Probabilistic frequency counter. Estimates how many times an element has been seen. Uses a 2D array (d rows × w columns) + d hash functions. INCREMENT(x): for each hash function i, increment array[i][hash_i(x) % w]. ESTIMATE(x): return min(array[i][hash_i(x) % w]) for all i. Always OVERESTIMATES (never underestimates). Accuracy improves with larger d and w. USE: (1) Network traffic frequency estimation (count packets per IP). (2) Top-K heavy hitters (find most frequent search queries). (3) Live stream analytics (approximate word counts).

Estimates cardinality (count of distinct elements) in O(1) memory. Counting unique visitors to a website: with a set, you'd need memory proportional to the number of unique visitors. HLL uses ~12 KB of memory to count up to billions of unique elements with < 1% error. INTERNAL: hash each element → look at the binary representation → count the position of the first 1 bit (leading zeros). The intuition: seeing many leading zeros is increasingly rare. If the maximum leading zeros seen is 10, there are approximately 2^10 = 1024 unique elements. To reduce variance, split the hash into m buckets (registers), compute per-bucket estimates, and take the harmonic mean. Redis: PFADD, PFCOUNT, PFMERGE (merge multiple HLLs = union of sets). USE CASES: (1) Unique visitor counting (Redis HLL). (2) Google BigQuery approximate_count_distinct(). (3) Network monitoring (unique IP counts).

examples.title: Failure Modes & Exception Handling
examples.description: How to handle catastrophic failures and network partitions in this tier.
examples.code:
try-catch fallback mechanics:
1. NetworkTimeoutException: Trigger circuit breaker and return stale cached data.
2. ConnectionRefusedException: Shift traffic to the standby region (Pilot Light architecture).
3. OOMError: Restart exact instance via Kubernetes Health Probes.

key_concepts.definition: Encode a (latitude, longitude) pair into a string by alternating bit representation of latitude and longitude ranges, then base32 encoding. 'dpz83' represents a rectangular area. Longer strings = smaller area = more precision. 4 characters ≈ 40×20 km. 6 characters ≈ 600×600 m. 8 characters ≈ 20×20 m. KEY PROPERTY: geohashes with a common prefix are geographically close. So proximity search = prefix match query (efficient with B-Tree index). EDGE CASE: boundary problem — two nearby points on opposite sides of a boundary have entirely different geohashes. FIX: search the 8 neighboring geohash cells too. USED BY: Elasticsearch geo_point, Redis GEOADD (uses sorted set with geohash as score).

Recursively divide a 2D space into 4 quadrants. Each node has 4 children (NW, NE, SW, SE). A leaf node contains up to K points. When a leaf exceeds K, split into 4 children and redistribute points. SEARCH (find points within a rectangle): start at root, for each child check if the child's bounding box intersects the search rectangle, recursively search intersecting children. TIME: O(log N) for well-distributed points. USED BY: Uber for finding nearby drivers. Yelp for nearby restaurants. Game engines for spatial indexing. CONFIGURABLE: max depth, max points per leaf, dynamic rebalancing.

Similar to B-Tree but for multi-dimensional data. Each node contains a bounding rectangle that encompasses all its children. Used by PostGIS (Postgres spatial extension) for spatial queries. Supports: point-in-polygon, nearest-neighbor, range queries. More general than Quadtree — works with arbitrary rectangles and polygons, not just points.

examples.title: Uber's Geospatial Architecture: From Quadtrees to H3
examples.description: How Uber scales location matching for millions of drivers and riders using hexagonal hierarchical spatial indexing.
examples.code:
The Problem:
Uber needs to instantly match a rider with the nearest 5 drivers. Calculating the Haversine distance (great-circle distance) between the rider and every single 100,000 active drivers in a city requires enormous CPU overhead.

The Evolution:
1. Early Days (Quadtrees): Uber initially used Quadtrees to segment the map into squares. A quadtree node would split when it held too many drivers. To find drivers, Uber queried the quadtree node containing the rider.
2. The Flaw with Squares: Bounding boxes are squares. Searching 'within a radius' on a square grid means the diagonal corners are further away than the edges, causing inaccurate distance sorting.
3. The Innovation (H3): Uber invented H3, an open-source Hexagonal Hierarchical Spatial Index. Hexagons are the closest shape to a circle that can seamlessly tile a flat plane. 

The Architecture:
When a driver pings their GPS location, Uber's backend calculates the H3 Hexagon ID for that lat/long. It stores the driver in a Redis cluster keyed by the Hexagon ID. When a rider opens the app, Uber calculates the rider's Hexagon ID and fetches all drivers in that hexagon (and the 6 immediately adjacent hexagons) from Redis in O(1) time.

Takeaway for Interviews:
Never calculate distances against raw coordinates in a database (e.g., `SELECT * WHERE distance(lat, lon) < 5`). Always use a spatial index (Geohash, Quadtree, H3) to map 2D coordinates into a 1D string/integer, allowing O(1) lookups in standard K-V stores or B-Trees.

examples.title: Spatial Data Structure Decision Matrix
examples.description: Use this matrix to justify your geospatial architecture in systems like Uber, Yelp, or Tinder.
examples.code:
ARCHITECTURE                   | INTERNAL MECHANISM           | ACCURACY | BEST USED FOR
-------------------------------|------------------------------|----------|-----------------------------------------------------
PostGIS (R-Tree)               | Tree of Bounding Boxes       | Perfect  | Complex polygons, traditional GIS, exact boundaries
Geohash (Elasticsearch/Redis)  | Z-Order Curve (Base32 String)| Low-Med  | "Points of interest within X miles" (Yelp, Tinder)
Quadtree                       | Splitting Squares            | Medium   | Dynamic densities (dense cities vs sparse rural)
H3 (Hexagonal Grid)            | Hexagons with identical radii| High     | Distance-critical sweeping algorithms (Uber, Lyft)

key_concepts.definition: Binary tree of hashes. Leaf nodes = hash(data chunk). Parent nodes = hash(left_child + right_child). Root hash summarizes ALL data. If any chunk changes, the root hash changes. COMPARISON: to find which chunks differ between two replicas: compare root hashes. If different, compare children recursively. Only need to exchange O(log N) hashes to find the differing chunk. USED BY: Cassandra (anti-entropy repair — find inconsistent data between replicas), Git (each commit is a Merkle tree of files), BitTorrent (verify downloaded pieces), Bitcoin (Merkle root in block header).

Tree where each edge represents a character. A path from root to a node represents a prefix. Each node stores whether it marks the end of a complete word/key. LOOKUP/INSERT: O(L) where L = key length (independent of N, number of keys). USE CASES: autocomplete (traverse to the prefix node, DFS to find all completions), IP routing (longest prefix matching), spell checking, phone contact search. COMPRESSED TRIE (Radix Tree): merge single-child chains. Reduces height and memory. Used by Linux kernel for routing tables.

Probabilistic sorted linked list with multiple levels. Bottom level = complete sorted list. Each higher level is a random subset (each element promoted with probability 1/2). SEARCH: start at top level, move right until next element > target, drop down a level, repeat. Average O(log N). INSERT: insert in bottom level, flip a coin to decide promotion to each higher level. WHY: achieves O(log N) search/insert like a balanced tree but much simpler to implement, especially for concurrent access (no tree rotations). USED BY: Redis sorted sets (ZSET), LevelDB/RocksDB memtable.
